newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel says debt terms talks advancing.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel says debt terms talks advancing.

text.p: Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA/Plc on Wednesday said debt restructuring talks with a banking consortium were making progress but were not yet completed.

Participating banks confirmed that there had been progress in the talks aimed at setting final terms for restructuring the tunnel operator's nine billion pounds ($14.6 billion) of debt but said the outcome was as yet uncertain.
"Our conversations with the banks are continuing and advancing very well but we cannot confirm at the moment that we have reached an agreement," a Eurotunnel spokeswoman said.
The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that the steering committee of leading bankers had agreed final terms.
But a banking source said: "I think that's a bit premature. It's not that simple."

The Eurotunnel spokeswoman said the tunnel operator could not speak for the banks but that in any case final terms would still have to be approved by other banks in the consortium as well as Eurotunnel's own board.
Officials of the steering committee's leading banks all declined comment on the report, saying they feared public discussion could sink an eventual pact.
But banking sources said the steering committee's 20 instructing banks would meet to weigh the deal's terms prior to April 24, when Eurotunnel plans to release its 1996 results.
The terms would then have to be approved by the remainder of the 225 lender banks, the Eurotunnel board and shareholders at a special July shareholder meeting.
"Even after the banks agree, the shareholders must be convinced that this deal is still in their own interests," said one analyst who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"So there has been progress but many questions remain unanswered. There is still a long way to go," the analyst said.

Analysts said a key question hanging over the restructuring talks was an expected report by safety authorities on new safety procedures adopted by Eurotunnel following a November 18 fire in the tunnel which slightly injured 34 people.
The blaze on board a train carrying a truck badly damaged and forced the closure of one of two rail tunnels. Eurotunnel hopes to complete repairs on the south tunnel by mid-May.

Eurotunnel officials have said they were confident the revised safety procedures announced earlier this month would be approved by the Anglo-French Channel Tunnel Safety Authority, which was expected to issue its own report on the blaze soon.
However, "if there is any suggestion that the (safety panel) wants major safety changes, this has major ramifications for the debt talks," said analyst Jeff Summers of London's Klesch & Co.
The fire had cast a shadow over the debt talks after restructuring was agreed in principle with steering committee banks last October.
The company triggered the debt restructuring after invoking a debt standstill in September 1995, since extended.
Despite the standstill, traders said a lively secondary market had emerged in Eurotunnel debt, with it being bid at about 43.5 cents on the dollar at this time.

The market had trended upwards in the last few weeks in anticipation of news about the restructuring talks, the traders said, rising as high as 45 to 46 cents on the dollar from levels of around 41 cents.

Some of the lender banks have demanded a formalised secondary market and "an official quotation system for the debt instruments could well emerge as part of the debt restructuring plan," one banking source told Reuters.
Establishment of a formal secondary market could encourage reluctant banks to accept the restructuring plan by making it easier for them to sell off their Eurotunnel debt once the pact was in place.
